topic: S4 Embodied, ramp assignment: robot production ramps and the robots-build-robots loop (humanoid and general-purpose robot capacity, industrial robot base, supply-chain bottlenecks, historical ramp analogues, fleet size 2028/2029/2031 under slow/base/fast ramps, robot labor share, and how far robots can shorten the doubling time of robot production itself)
scenario_context: S4 Embodied = S3 Recursive cognition plus general-purpose robotics deployed at scale, including robots helping build robots, factories, labs, test stands and infrastructure. This file covers only the production-ramp side: how many capable robots can exist, when, and what binds their growth. Gate-by-gate physical compression is handled in sibling files; a preliminary Amdahl adjustment is given under implications_for_space_tree.
key_findings: Robotics is already bleeding into the physical world fast in percentage terms but from a tiny base. Global humanoid shipments went from roughly 2,300 (2024) to 13,318 (2025, Omdia) to 19,000-25,000 in H1 2026 alone (Smart Analytics, Counterpoint, IDC); 2026 full-year is forecast at 50,000-100,000 (TrendForce >50k, Goldman 75k, BofA 90k; China MIIT expects >100k domestic output). That is an output doubling time of about 4-5 months, the fastest of any analogue in this file except Model 3's first year and the Liberty ship mobilization.

The installed general-purpose fleet is still about 0.1 million units at end-2026 (most of them small, research, education, demo or pilot units) against 5.0 million industrial robots (IFR, end-2025) and roughly 460 million manufacturing workers worldwide. The IFR counts only about 7,000 full-size (>140 cm) humanoids sold for professional use in 2025 and says most applications are pilots that often need human teleoperation. Musk said on the Q4 2025 call (Jan 28, 2026) that no Optimus was doing useful work in Tesla factories.

Company targets slip hard in the West and are roughly met in China. Tesla's 2025 target of 5,000-10,000 Optimus units ended at a few hundred (<10%); Gen 3 production slipped from early 2026 to late July/August 2026; reported rate several hundred per week by August (The Information, unverified) against a 1 million per year Fremont design. Agility's 2023 RoboFab was sized for 10,000 per year; Omdia credits Agility with about 150 units in 2025. Figure's BotQ line is rated 12,000 per year; it built its 1,000th Figure 03 in July 2026 at about one per hour. Chinese makers (AgiBot, Unitree, UBTech) met or beat their 2025 numbers, which is why bank forecasts are being revised up (Goldman 2030 from 256k to 890k; Morgan Stanley China 2026 from 14k to 28k to 50k).

Every historical ramp shows the same shape: 3-8 month output doublings for 1-3 years from a small base, then deceleration to 1-3 year doublings within 3-5 years as a downstream gate binds. US military aircraft 1940-42 doubled every ~6.5 months and 1940-44 every ~10 months (3,611 to 96,270) under total mobilization; BYD NEVs 2020-22 every ~7 months then ~28 months; Model T 1909-13 every ~12 months then ~35 months; smartphones ~16-24 months; Li-ion ~23 months; Starlink satellites ~4 years (launch-bound); FANUC robot output ~7 years despite lights-out robots-building-robots since 2001 (demand-bound).

Fleet projections (active general-purpose robots, end-year): slow 0.24M (2028), 0.49M (2029), 1.4M (2031); base 0.76M, 2.0M, 9.0M; fast 1.6M, 4.6M, 24M. Annual shipments in 2031: 0.5M / 4.5M / 13M. Base is 64x in five years (10-month doubling), i.e. WWII aircraft mobilization pace sustained for five years; fast (8.5-month doubling, 132x) exceeds every peacetime analogue. Bank consensus for 2030 (0.45-1.2M shipments) sits between slow and base.

In the base S4 ramp the whole general-purpose fleet only reaches the size of today's industrial robot stock (~8-9M) in 2031. Robot labor by 2031: about 1.3% of global manufacturing labor in base (4.6% fast, 0.1% slow), 0.2% of construction (0.8% fast), 5% of lab technician labor and 6% of aerospace production labor in base (16-20% fast). Concentrated deployment (e.g. 25% of the fleet in the US) gives about 11% of US manufacturing labor in base and 30% in fast by 2031. Robots are a big minority in chosen factories by 2031, not the economy-wide workforce.

The binding constraints on robot output through 2031 are not chips, batteries or energy. A million humanoids need about 2.3 GWh of batteries (0.1% of the 2,280 GWh of Li-ion shipped in 2025), 2-4.5 kt of NdFeB (about 1% of ~330 kt), about 1 million 130 W edge computers, and about 1.5 TWh a year of electricity. The binding ones are precision actuator parts (planetary roller screws, about 20% of BOM, thread-grinding capacity tight through 2027-28; harmonic reducers, Leaderdrive about 1M to 2M a year 2026-27, HDS about 2.2M a year, against ~14 or more per humanoid), dexterous hands (Tesla's stated top bottleneck), reliability and usefulness (UBTech Walker S2 at 30-50% of human output; Figure 02 forearm failures), heavy-rare-earth export licensing (in force since April 2025; the Nov 2025 pause of the October measures lapses about Nov 10, 2026), and the business case.

Magnets become a volume constraint only in the fast ramp after 2031: 138M robots a year (fast, 2035) at 2-4.5 kg would need 276-621 kt of NdFeB, 0.8-1.9x all 2025 world output. Base 2035 (30M a year) needs 59-133 kt, 18-40% of 2025 output, so magnet capacity must roughly double by the mid-2030s.

The robots-build-robots loop shortens the doubling time of robot production by about 1.5-2x, not 10x, before 2031-2035. Labor is a small share of the constraint: 4.5M humanoids a year at an estimated 100-300 supply-chain labor hours each is only 0.2-0.7M FTE, which 1-3% of the 2031 base fleet could replace. The loop's real leverage is removing the hiring and training lag (Willow Run needed 42,000 workers and ~18 months to reach rate) and running existing capital 24/7, which roughly halves capital per unit of output. What it cannot shorten before robots also build machine tools, sintering furnaces, fabs, mines and buildings: precision-tool lead times of 6-14 months, factory construction (~9-12 months even at Giga Shanghai speed), hardware-generation cycles of ~12-30 months to fix wear-out failures, and capital and permits.

Quantitatively, if the loop holds the production doubling time at ~9 months from 2029 instead of letting it decay to ~15 months, it adds about 2x to the 2031 fleet but about 9x by 2035 (2^(72/9-72/15)). With 6 versus 12 months it is 4x by 2031 and 64x by 2035. The loop needs a base of roughly 1M capable units and S3-grade cognition (2028+) before it compounds, so it is a 2030s accelerator; by 2031 it matters inside the robot makers and a few flagship factories.

Forethought's Industrial Explosion note (May 2025) reaches the same order of magnitude from first principles: initial robot-economy doubling times of about 1 year or less with abundant AI cognitive labor (capital-productivity approach ~2 years naive, 2-4x faster with AI; humanoid payback ~5 months raw, 1-2 years after factory costs), 'on the order of a few years' in the real world, versus 6 years for the last doubling of the world robot stock. Its days-to-weeks doubling is a long-run physical upper bound, not a 2031 claim.

For the Space Unlock Tree: S4 robotics mainly changes the production-ramp, fabrication and integration-labor slices (more shifts, no hiring lag, faster line learning), not launch, qualification statistics, thermal-vacuum time constants or regulatory clocks. Raising the S3 physical multipliers from 1.3/1.5/1.5x to 1.5-1.8x (fabrication), 1.6-1.8x (integration and test), 1.5-1.6x (qualification) lifts the Amdahl ceiling from ~51% to ~55-60%. Because the 2031 base fleet covers only ~6% of aerospace production labor, the realized gain by 2031 is a few points over S3 for most programs and larger only for vertically integrated players that deploy their own robots (Tesla/SpaceX-type).

slip_rule_of_thumb: US humanoid startups and Tesla have realized 1-25% of announced first-period volume and ~2x stated timelines; Chinese leaders have met or beaten theirs, which is why bank forecasts were revised up 1.5-3.5x during 2026 while company timelines in the US slipped. analogue_synthesis: Peak-phase output doublings of 2.5-7 months last 1-3 years from a small base; sustained 4-5 year ramps of complex machines top out at ~10-month doublings (WWII aircraft) and only under national mobilization; peacetime industries decelerate to 12-36 month doublings by year 3-5. The base S4 ramp (10-month doubling 2026-31) is therefore the WWII-mobilization pace sustained for five years, justified only if S3/S4 cognition makes robots useful enough that demand behaves like wartime demand (as AI datacenter demand did in 2024-26). The fast ramp (8.5-month doubling, 132x) has no peacetime precedent at this complexity.

fleet_projections.method: Annual global shipments of general-purpose robots (humanoids plus mobile manipulators) from 2026 levels with year-on-year multipliers; active fleet = shipments within service life (2 years for pre-2027 vintages, 5 years after). slow.label: S2-like: bank consensus with typical slip; robots stay narrow and half-productive

base.label: S4 central: S3 cognition makes robots broadly useful from 2028; Tesla Fremont at rate by 2029, Texas line from 2027-28; China doubling yearly

fast.label: S4 with working robots-build-robots loop and wartime-style capital mobilization; Musk-scale targets met with ~1-2 year slip

fleet_projections.unconditional_view: Outside the S4 premise, the slow ramp is the most likely path (~50%), base ~35%, fast ~15%.
fleet_projections.cross_checks: Bank consensus for 2030 shipments (MS China 446k; Goldman 890k global; BofA 1.2M) lies between slow (367k) and base (2.5M). Announced nameplate by 2028 (Tesla Fremont 1M, China leaders several hundred thousand, Figure 12-50k) supports ~1M/yr output in 2029 at ~50% utilization, consistent with base 1.26M. Base fleet matches today's industrial robot stock (~8-9M projected for 2031 at 9%/yr) only in 2031.

robot_labor_share.assumptions: Fleet allocation: manufacturing incl. in-plant logistics 45%, warehousing/logistics 25%, construction 4%, lab work 2%, aerospace production 1%, other/services 23% (cf. Counterpoint 2027 installs: warehousing 33%, auto 24%, manufacturing 15%, retail 12%). Human-equivalent FTE per robot (shifts x relative productivity): slow 0.4 (2028), 0.5 (2029), 0.8 (2031); base 0.6, 1.0, 1.5; fast 0.8, 1.2, 2.0. Starting point: UBTech Walker S2 at 30-50% of human output, mostly single shift. Workforces: manufacturing ~460M, construction ~250M (sourced); lab technicians ~5M and aerospace production ~2M worldwide (general, estimate); US manufacturing ~12.7M, construction ~8.3M, aerospace products and parts ~0.53M (general).
robot_labor_share.concentrated_US_case: If the US hosts 25% of the fleet: US manufacturing 1.7% (base 2029), 11% (base 2031), 30% (fast 2031); US aerospace production at 2% of the US fleet 11% (base 2031) to 31% (fast 2031); US construction 1.6% (base 2031). Individual vertically integrated firms (Tesla, SpaceX, BYD, Xiaomi-type) can be far above these averages.
robot_labor_share.context: Industrial robots already equal ~1.3% of manufacturing headcount by count (132 per 10,000 employees worldwide; 12% in Korea) but each does one narrow task.
robot_labor_share.verdict: By 2031 general-purpose robots are a large minority in chosen factories, labs and production lines, and a rounding error in global construction. Economy-wide significance (10-30% of manufacturing labor) arrives ~2033-2035 in base, ~2031-2032 in fast, after 2035 in slow.

self_replication_loop.question: How much can robots shorten the doubling time of robot production itself?
self_replication_loop.evidence_that_loop_alone_is_not_enough: FANUC has run lights-out robots-building-robots since 2001 and its output still doubled only every ~7 years: demand-bound. Tesla's 2017-18 Model 3 over-automation slowed the ramp. Figure, UBTech and Agility plan humanoids in their own lines; in 2026 humanoids there move materials (depalletizing, loading) while cobots do final assembly screws (UBTech Liuzhou).

doubling_time_decomposition.today: 12-18 months per large plant (Willow Run 42,000 workers, ~18 months to rate)

doubling_time_decomposition.component: Precision machine tools and component capacity
doubling_time_decomposition.today: 6-14 month lead times; reducer capacity ~1 year per doubling
doubling_time_decomposition.compressible: Little until robots build machine tools (2030s)

doubling_time_decomposition.component: Hardware generation to fix reliability and capability
doubling_time_decomposition.with_S4_loop_2030: ~9-15 months (fleet-parallel field testing, AI redesign); tooling and validation floor ~6-12 months

doubling_time_decomposition.component: Materials (rare earths, copper, steel), chips, permits
doubling_time_decomposition.today: 2-15 years for new mines and plants; fabs 2-3 years (general)
Forethought: ~1-2 yr doubling with factory costs; humanoid raw payback ~5 months
doubling_time_decomposition.with_S4_loop_2030: ~0.5-1 yr if robots are ~1.5 FTE and priced ~$20-30k

self_replication_loop.labor_arithmetic: Robot-production labor is small: 4.5M humanoids a year (base 2031) at an estimated 100-300 supply-chain labor hours each is 0.45-1.35B hours, ~0.2-0.7M FTE. Replacing half of that takes ~70-230k robots at 1.5 FTE, i.e. 1-3% of the 2031 base fleet. So the loop is cheap to close on the labor side; its limit is the capital-goods chain and reliability iteration, not labor.

doubling_time_estimates.observed_2024_2026: ~4-5 months (small base, demand and funding pulled by China)
doubling_time_estimates.no_loop_trajectory: Decelerates to ~12-18 months by 2029-31 (every analogue's year 3-5 behavior)
doubling_time_estimates.with_loop_best_case_fast: ~6-8 months, comparable to WWII aircraft 1940-42 and BYD 2020-22
doubling_time_estimates.floor_before_2035: ~6 months, set by factory construction, machine-tool lead times and hardware-generation cycles
doubling_time_estimates.long_run_upper_bound: Days to weeks (Forethought), requiring robots to build every link from mines to fabs; not before 2035

self_replication_loop.loop_effect_on_fleet: If the loop holds doubling at 9 months from 2029 instead of decaying to 15 months: 2^(24/9 - 24/15) = ~2.1x fleet by 2031; 2^(72/9 - 72/15) = ~9x by 2035. With 6 vs 12 months: 4x by 2031, 64x by 2035. With 12 vs 18 months: 1.6x by 2031, 4x by 2035.
self_replication_loop.when_it_starts_to_matter: Needs (a) S3-grade cognition for general manipulation (2028 in the main model), (b) a fleet of ~1M capable units (base 2029, fast 2028, slow after 2031), and (c) robots able to assemble hands, actuators and machine tools. Inside robot makers' own lines: 2028-2029. Across the robot supply chain (reducers, screws, motors): ~2030-2032. Up the capital-goods chain (machine tools, furnaces, fabs, construction): mid-2030s.
self_replication_loop.verdict_2031_vs_2035: By 2031 the loop roughly doubles the fleet relative to no-loop in base and is visible mainly inside robot makers and flagship factories; it does not make robots a large share of global labor. By 2035 it is the dominant driver: 5-10x fleet difference, tens of millions of robots in base, and robot labor at 10-30% of manufacturing in the leading economies.

what_robotics_compresses: Hiring and training of production labor: from 12-18 months per large plant to near zero once skills copy as software (largest robotics-specific gain; S4 from ~2029).
Shift utilization: 24/7 operation of existing factories, test stands and labs raises output per unit capital ~1.5-2x and removes overtime and fatigue limits.
Line learning: rated output reached in ~3-6 months instead of 12-18 months when robots and AI tune processes continuously (BotQ already went 1/day to 1/hour in 4 months).

Reliability learning for mass-produced hardware: fleet-parallel field hours and 24/7 accelerated life testing shorten wear-out discovery (works for robots, cars, satellites built by the thousand; not for rare flights).

Production-rate ramps of engines, stages and satellites that are labor- and line-learning-limited: model gate 'Production ramp' S3 0.7-0.8x could go to ~0.5-0.7x for 2030-31 programs with robotized lines (estimate).

Fabrication and integration labor in high-mix, low-rate aerospace work (the slice humanoids target): physical multipliers ~1.5-1.8x by 2031 versus S3's 1.3-1.5x, for firms that deploy robots at scale.

Lab experiment throughput where human technician hours bind (sample prep, assays, assembly of test articles): 2-3x more experiments per facility per year (estimate), within the physics time constants of each experiment.
Brownfield factory conversion and line installation (Fremont S/X line removed in 46 days).
what_robotics_cannot_compress: Physics time constants: curing, sintering, heat treatment, thermal-vacuum soak, creep and fatigue exposure, propellant conditioning; a robot runs them 24/7 but cannot make them shorter.
Statistics: confidence needs trials or accepted priors (~230 zero-failure trials for 0.99 at 90% confidence); robots make trials cheaper, not fewer.
Launch windows, orbital mechanics, flight-test cadence and the launch gate that already caps Starlink output.
Biology's own clocks: cell growth, animal studies, clinical trial follow-up.
Upstream materials: rare-earth mines (7-15 years, general), separation and magnet plants outside China (2-4 years), copper, gallium; heavy rare-earth licensing is political.
Machine-tool, fab and furnace lead times (6-36 months) until robots build those too (2030s).
Greenfield construction of factories, pads and plants (concrete cure, steel erection, utility interconnects) before construction robots mature (after 2031 for most work).
Institutions: permits, NEPA, FAA licensing, safety standards for humanoids near people (IFR cites standardized safety as a precondition), insurance, labor law and politics.
Capital formation at the fast-ramp scale (~$300B+ a year of robot purchases by 2031) and the business case where wages are low.
The minimum time of a hardware generation (design freeze, tooling, validation): ~6-12 months even with S3 design speed.

implications_for_space_tree.production_ramp_gate: S3 0.7-0.8x to S4 ~0.5-0.7x for programs ramping in 2030-31 at robot-heavy firms; ~0.7x elsewhere (estimate).
implications_for_space_tree.long_lead_parts_gate: S3 0.8-0.9x to S4 0.75-0.85x (more shifts at forges and machine shops; capacity and single sources still bind).
implications_for_space_tree.pad_and_plant_construction_gate: S3 0.8-0.9x to S4 0.75-0.85x before 2031 (construction robots immature); larger gains after 2032.
implications_for_space_tree.amdahl_adjustment: Holding S3 cognitive speedups (20x/50x/20x) and raising physical multipliers to fabrication 1.5-1.8x, integration and test 1.6-1.8x, qualification 1.5-1.6x, launch 1.0x gives a schedule-compression ceiling of ~55-60% (2.2-2.5x) versus S3's ~51% (2.0x). Realized by 2031 for typical programs: S3 realized (35-45%) plus ~2-5 points, because the 2031 base fleet covers only ~6% of global aerospace production labor; vertically integrated robot users could approach the ceiling.
implications_for_space_tree.timing: S4 robotics effects on space hardware start ~2029 (base fleet ~2M, S3 cognition available), become material in 2030-31 at a few firms, and broad only after 2032.

signposts: Audited humanoid output: Tesla reporting Optimus units built and in productive use (watch Q3 2026 call, late Oct 2026, and Q4 2026); >1,000/week at Fremont by end-2026 would put Tesla on the base path.
Full-year 2026 global shipments: <50k = slow; 70-100k = base; >150k = fast.
Published productivity and uptime KPIs: humanoids at >=80% of human output on paid tasks (UBTech's 2027 target) and multi-shift operation without teleoperation.
China's Nov 10, 2026 rare-earth decision: re-imposition or extension of the suspended measures; non-China magnet capacity announcements.
Roller-screw and reducer capacity: Leaderdrive >2M annualized in 2027; thread-grinding lead times falling below 6 months.
First documented line where humanoids do final assembly of humanoids (not just material handling) at Figure BotQ, Tesla or UBTech.
Giga Texas Optimus line producing meaningful volume by summer 2027.
Bank forecast revisions: Goldman/BofA 2030 shipments rising above ~1.5M would signal convergence on the base ramp.
Humanoid safety standards (ISO work on dynamically stable mobile manipulators) and first insurance products for unfenced operation.
timeline_view: 2026-2027: steep but tiny. Humanoid output keeps doubling every ~4-6 months (2026 ~50-100k shipped, mostly Chinese, mostly pilots); global fleet ~0.1-0.3M against 5M industrial robots; no meaningful labor share anywhere; Tesla and Figure lines ramping with US-style slips. 2028-2029: the usual deceleration point. In slow it arrives (0.2-0.5M fleet); in base S3 cognition makes robots useful and the fleet reaches ~0.8M (2028) and ~2M (2029); robots-build-robots begins inside robot makers' lines; roller screws, reducers and hands bind. 2030-2031: base fleet ~4.5M (2030) and ~9M (2031), about the size of today's industrial robot stock; ~1-1.5% of global manufacturing labor, ~5-6% of lab and aerospace production labor, ~11% of US manufacturing if the US hosts a quarter of the fleet; fast reaches ~24M. The loop roughly doubles the 2031 fleet versus no-loop. 2032-2035: the loop compounds (5-10x fleet difference by 2035), base reaches tens of millions (~70M), robot labor reaches 10-30% of manufacturing in leading economies, magnets and capital become the volume constraints, and construction and infrastructure start to feel it. So the answer to 'quickly' is: yes in growth rate, not in share, before 2031; economy-wide physical acceleration is a 2032-2035 story.
strongest_case_fast: Humanoid output has grown ~5-6x a year for two years, Chinese makers beat their own targets, and banks keep revising up (Goldman 2030 +3.5x in one revision). Capital is not binding (Tesla >$25B capex, Unitree IPO, $4.3B of 2025 funding), batteries, chips and energy are not binding at millions of units, and Chinese actuator prices fell ~80% in 2025 as capacity flooded in. If S3 cognition makes a humanoid worth 1.5-2 human FTEs by 2029 at a $20-30k unit price, payback falls under a year everywhere, demand becomes wartime-like, and robots can staff their own lines 24/7 with no hiring lag. WWII aircraft (26.7x in 4 years) and BYD (9.8x in 2 years) show complex-machine output can sustain 6-10 month doublings; adding a robots-build-robots loop could hold that pace past the usual year-3 deceleration, giving ~13M robots a year and ~24M in service by 2031, ~20% of aerospace and lab labor, and a robot economy doubling in ~6-8 months by the early 2030s.
strongest_case_slow: Every historical ramp decelerates within 3-5 years, and humanoids have not yet shown usefulness: the IFR counts only ~7,000 full-size professional units in 2025 and calls the business case weak with frequent teleoperation; Musk conceded in Jan 2026 that no Optimus did useful work; UBTech's best robots run at 30-50% of human output; Figure 02's forearm failed in an 11-month pilot. Western nameplate has been 1-25% realized (Agility ~1.5%, Tesla 2025 <10%). Precision roller screws, reducers and hands are capacity-limited through 2027-28, heavy rare earths are licensed by China, and FANUC's 25 years of robots-building-robots never produced faster than ~7-year doublings because demand, not production, binds. On this view the fleet is ~0.5M in 2029 and ~1.4M in 2031, robot labor is ~0.1% of global manufacturing, and the space tree's S3 physical multipliers (1.3-1.5x) are if anything generous.
caveats: Shipment counts differ by up to 3x across Omdia, IDC, Counterpoint, Smart Analytics, IFR and MIIT because of definitions (size, shipments vs production, consumer vs professional).
